Chapter Three: Discovering Personal Type — The Self-Assessment Process.
So, you already know that personality plays a big role in feeling satisfied at work. But here’s the big question—how do you actually figure out your own type? It’s not as simple as checking a few boxes on some online quiz. Instead, it’s about honest self-reflection, paying attention to your own patterns, and sometimes, getting feedback from people who know you well.
Let’s talk about the self-discovery journey. It starts with exploring the four key preference pairs. Imagine asking yourself, do you feel energized or drained by social gatherings? When you notice something, is it the little details that grab your attention, or do you zoom out and see the big picture? When you make decisions, do you focus on pros and cons, or do you care more about how everyone feels? And finally, are you more comfortable planning everything in advance, or do you prefer to go with the flow?
Sometimes, it helps to think back to when you were a kid—before you started worrying about what others expected from you. Those early interests usually show your true instincts. Maybe you loved organizing your toys and making lists. That probably points to a Judging preference. Or maybe you were the creative one, always making up new games on the spot—chances are, you leaned toward Perceiving.
Of course, there are a few common traps to watch out for. It’s easy to confuse what comes naturally with what you’ve learned to do because of your job or society’s expectations. For example, maybe you became comfortable leading meetings because you had to, not because you’re naturally outgoing. The important thing is to notice the difference between what feels truly you, and what you’ve picked up along the way.
Sometimes, you need a little outside perspective to get it right. Trusted friends, family, or coworkers can help by pointing out patterns you might miss. Like, maybe your friend notices that you always try to keep everyone happy during group projects—hinting that you might have a Feeling preference.
Now, what about formal assessment tools? They can be helpful, but they work best when you combine them with your own reflections. The idea isn’t to just accept whatever label you get—it’s about using those results as a jumping-off point to dig deeper. And honestly, it’s totally normal to feel unsure about a preference or two, especially if you’ve had to adapt to different situations in life.
Once you figure out your four main preferences, you get your full type—like ENFP or ISTJ. Each type comes with its own strengths, motivations, and even a few challenges. When you really understand your type, it’s like having a personalized map for exploring careers that actually fit. For example, if you’re someone who prefers Intuition and Perceiving, rigid routines might feel suffocating, but creative, open-ended projects? Those probably light you up. Suddenly, choosing a career isn’t just about chasing a paycheck—it’s about finding something that feels right on the inside.
Here’s the real value of self-awareness: It’s not about boxing yourself in, but about getting clear on what really matters to you. When you know your strengths and values, you can make choices that feel authentic. Plus, having this insight gives you a new way to understand—and appreciate—the differences in people around you. That means less conflict and more empathy, whether you’re at work or at home.
